column2: Fighter
This person has been drilled in the basics of combat and can hold their own in a brawl or a press of soldiers, but they are no champion.
Warrior
This person is a seasoned fighter, blooded in real fighting rather than the training yard. They are the sort of soldier others follow into a breach.
Master
This person has mastered the warrior's craft. Few who face them in single combat walk away, and their name carries weight among soldiers.
Grandmaster
This person is one of the finest warriors of their age, a name that soldiers speak with awe. Without bending, they have still made themselves a legend of the battlefield.
Train in the Warrior's Arts
Take this child out to the yard and drill them in the craft of arms. They can climb as high as you have climbed and no further. Only a Grandmaster can make another.
Master My Weapon
[This.GetTitledFirstName] means to master the craft of arms. Every drill, every bout, every battle is a lesson, and [This.GetSheHe] will climb as high as a non-bender can.
The ambition consumes your days. Every free hour finds you in the yard, and the household guard have learned to give you room when you are in a mind to drill.
Drill until your arms ache.
Push yourself past exhaustion.
There are other matters to see to.
The drills have finally taken hold. You can hold your own in a press now, a Fighter by any honest reckoning.
It is a start.
What the yard could not teach, hard fighting has. You are a Warrior now, the sort of soldier others follow into a breach.
Good.
Few in the realm can match you blade to blade. You have become a Master of the warrior's craft, and your name carries weight among soldiers.
Let them come.
There is no one left who can teach you anything about killing. You are a Grandmaster, a legend of the battlefield, made without a drop of bending.
They will sing of this.
The yard has paid for itself. Your pupil's strikes come faster and truer than they did a season ago, and the lessons have finally begun to stick.
They are coming along.
A season of hard drilling, and little to show for it. Your pupil learns the forms well enough, but they have not yet become instinct.
Keep at it.
